lessons.title: What Data Communication Is
lessons.content:
Imagine you are sitting in a classroom in Rajshahi and your best friend sits three rows behind you. You want to tell her that the teacher is coming. You cannot shout, so you write a note, fold it, and pass it hand to hand down the row. Your note is the message. You are the sender. Your friend is the receiver. The chain of hands is the path the note travels on. And the rule you both agreed on earlier, like 'a folded note with a star on it means urgent', is the agreement that makes the message mean something. Without knowing it, you just used every part of a data communication system.

What data communication means: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through some kind of transmission medium, such as a wire, a glass fiber or the air. The word 'data' here means information written in a form that machines can store and move, usually as bits (0s and 1s). When your phone sends a photo to your cousin on WhatsApp, when an ATM in Chattogram checks your balance with a bank server in Dhaka, when a smart meter tells DESCO how much electricity you used, all of that is data communication. This course is about the bottom part of that journey: how bits are turned into signals, how signals travel, what spoils them on the way, and how the receiver gets the bits back correctly.

The four goals: A good communication system must do four things. Delivery: the data must reach the correct device and only that device. Accuracy: the data must arrive without being changed; a photo with random wrong bits is useless. Timeliness: the data must arrive in time; a voice call where words arrive two seconds late is painful. Jitter control: the delay should stay steady. If video packets arrive 30 ms apart, then 70 ms, then 10 ms, the picture stutters. Jitter means this unevenness in arrival time.

Component 1, the message: The message is the information you want to send. It can be text, numbers, pictures, sound, video, or a mix. A bKash payment request, a Facebook post and a Zoom class are all messages.

Component 2, the sender: The sender is the device that sends the message. It could be a laptop, a phone, a video camera, a server or even a temperature sensor in a garment factory.

Component 3, the receiver: The receiver is the device that gets the message. Again, it can be any device: a phone, a TV, a printer, a server.

Component 4, the transmission medium: The medium is the physical path the message takes from sender to receiver. Copper twisted-pair cable, coaxial cable, optical fiber and radio waves through air are the common ones. Later in the course we spend two whole lessons on media.

Component 5, the protocol: A protocol is a set of rules that controls the communication. It is an agreement between the devices. Two devices can be perfectly connected by a cable and still not understand each other, just like a person who speaks only Bangla and a person who speaks only Japanese can sit side by side and still not talk. The protocol decides the format of the data, what each part means, and when to send it.

How data is represented: Before we send anything we need to turn it into bits. Text: each character gets a number code. ASCII uses 7 bits per character, so it has 128 codes; the letter A is 65, which is 1000001 in binary. Unicode is a much bigger code that includes Bangla letters, emoji and almost every script in the world. Numbers: numbers are written directly in binary, so 13 becomes 1101. Images: a picture is a grid of tiny dots called pixels. A black and white pixel needs 1 bit. A colour pixel in RGB form uses three numbers, red, green and blue, often 8 bits each, so 24 bits per pixel. Audio: sound is a continuous wave, so we measure it many times per second and store each measurement as a number. Video: video is a series of pictures shown quickly, often 25 or 30 frames per second, plus audio.

A small worked example: How many bits is a 100 by 100 pixel colour picture with 24 bits per pixel? There are 100 x 100 = 10,000 pixels. Each needs 24 bits, so 10,000 x 24 = 240,000 bits. Dividing by 8 gives 30,000 bytes, about 30 kilobytes before any compression. Now you see why compression like JPEG matters: real photos have millions of pixels.

Data flow, direction matters: Communication between two devices can flow in three ways. Think of three kinds of roads.

Simplex: Data moves in one direction only, like a one-way street. One device only sends, the other only receives. A keyboard sending keys to a computer, or an old TV broadcast station sending to your TV, works this way. The whole capacity of the channel is used in that one direction.

Half-duplex: Both devices can send, but not at the same time. It is like a narrow bridge over a canal in a village where only one rickshaw can cross at a time; rickshaws from each side take turns. Walkie-talkies work like this: you press the button, talk, say 'over', and release so the other person can reply. When one side sends, the whole channel belongs to it.

Full-duplex: Both devices send and receive at the same time, like a two-lane road. A normal phone call is full-duplex: you and your friend can both talk at once, even if it is rude. The capacity is shared between the two directions, either by having two separate physical paths or by dividing the one channel.

What makes a network good: When many devices are connected, we judge the network by three criteria. Performance: how fast data travels and how quickly the network responds. We measure it with throughput (how many bits actually get through per second) and delay (how long a bit takes). These two often fight each other; pushing more data into a network can increase delay because of queues. Reliability: how often the network fails, how quickly it recovers, and how well it survives disasters such as a cyclone damaging towers. Security: protecting data from people who should not read or change it, and having plans to recover from attacks.

Real life example 1, a bKash payment: You pay 500 taka to a shop using bKash. The message is the payment request: amount, shop number and your PIN in encrypted form. The sender is your phone. The medium is first radio waves from your phone to a Grameenphone or Robi tower, then fiber cable from the tower to the operator's core network, then more fiber to bKash's servers. The receiver is the bKash server. The protocol is a stack of agreed rules, from how the radio signal is shaped up to how the payment request is formatted. The four goals all matter here: delivery (to bKash, not someone else), accuracy (500, not 5000), timeliness (the shop is waiting) and low jitter matters less here than in video.

Real life example 2, a cricket match on TV: When Bangladesh plays at Mirpur, cameras capture video. The broadcaster sends it by fiber or satellite uplink to a satellite, and the satellite sends it down to cable operators all over the country, who send it on coaxial or fiber cable to homes. Most of this path is simplex: the TV only receives. Timeliness and jitter matter a lot, because the picture must flow smoothly. Notice that one message travels across many different media, one after another, and each part has its own rules.

A tiny bit of history: People have sent data over distances for a long time. Drums and smoke signals were early ways to send short messages. In 1844 Samuel Morse sent a telegraph message over a wire between Washington and Baltimore, using short and long pulses (dots and dashes) for letters. That was already digital in spirit: only two kinds of symbols. In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell got his telephone patent, and voice travelled as an analog electrical signal. Later came radio, television, computer modems, and finally the internet and mobile networks. Every one of these uses the same five components; only the medium, the signals and the protocols changed. The ideas in this course are the ones that made each of these jumps possible.

Why study this as a computer science student: Every app you will ever build sends data somewhere. If you understand why a WiFi link slows down near a wall, why a fiber link is faster than copper, why errors happen and how they are caught, you will design better systems and debug faster. Jobs in telecom companies like Grameenphone, Robi, Banglalink and Teletalk, in internet service providers, in network engineering and in embedded systems all need this course. It is also the base for Computer Networks, which you study next.

What this course covers: First we look at networks and the layered model, so you know where each topic sits. Then signals: analog and digital, sine waves, bandwidth, and what spoils signals (attenuation, distortion, noise). Then the speed limits: Nyquist and Shannon formulas. Then encoding: how bits become voltage patterns (line coding, block coding, scrambling), how voice becomes bits (PCM), and how bits ride on radio waves (ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM). Then sharing a link (multiplexing and spread spectrum), the physical media themselves, switching, and the telephone and cable networks. Finally the data link layer: catching and fixing errors (parity, CRC, Hamming codes), framing, flow control, and how many devices share one medium (ALOHA, CSMA, Ethernet and WiFi ideas).

Common mistakes: Students often mix up the medium and the protocol. The medium is physical: a cable or the air. The protocol is a set of rules, which is not physical at all. Another mix-up is half-duplex versus full-duplex: in half-duplex both sides can send, just not at the same time; it is not 'only one side can send', that is simplex. A third one: 'data' and 'signal' are not the same thing. Data is the information; a signal is the physical form (a voltage, a light pulse, a radio wave) that carries it. We will separate these carefully in lesson 4.

What exams ask: Name the five components of a data communication system and explain each with an example. Distinguish simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex with examples. List the four fundamental characteristics (delivery, accuracy, timeliness, jitter). Calculate the number of bits needed for a simple image or a piece of text. Explain the network criteria of performance, reliability and security.

Recap: Data communication is moving data between devices over a medium. It has five components: message, sender, receiver, medium and protocol. It must deliver data to the right place, accurately, on time and with steady delay. Data of every kind becomes bits first. Data can flow simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex. In the next lesson we connect many devices together and see the shapes networks can take.
key_points: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices over a transmission medium such as copper, fiber or air.
Five components: message, sender, receiver, transmission medium and protocol (the agreed set of rules).
A good system gives delivery, accuracy, timeliness and low jitter (steady delay).
Text, numbers, images, audio and video are all turned into bits before sending; ASCII uses 7 bits per character, Unicode covers Bangla and more.
Simplex is one way only, half-duplex is both ways but taking turns, full-duplex is both ways at the same time.
Networks are judged on performance (throughput and delay), reliability and security.
Data is the information; a signal is the physical form that carries it.
lessons.tip: For every new topic in this course, ask yourself which of the five components it improves: the message, the sender, the receiver, the medium or the protocol. It keeps the big picture in your head.
lessons.task: Pick three things you use today (for example a phone call, YouTube and a TV remote). For each, write down the message, sender, receiver, medium and protocol, and decide whether the data flow is simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex.

quiz.q: Which of these is the protocol in a data communication system?
options: The copper cable between two computers
The set of rules both devices agree to follow
The server that receives the data
quiz.explain: A protocol is the agreement (rules for format, meaning and timing). The cable is the medium, the photo is the message and the server is the receiver.

quiz.q: A walkie-talkie where only one person can talk at a time uses which data flow?
quiz.explain: Both sides can send, but they take turns, so it is half-duplex.

quiz.q: How many bits does a 10 by 10 pixel colour image need at 24 bits per pixel, without compression?
quiz.explain: 10 x 10 = 100 pixels, and 100 x 24 = 2,400 bits.

quiz.q: Video packets arrive with very uneven gaps, so the picture stutters. Which characteristic is poor?
quiz.explain: Jitter is the variation in arrival delay. Uneven gaps mean high jitter.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Data and signal mean exactly the same thing
A signal is the physical form, like a voltage or radio wave, that carries data
The medium is a set of software rules
Simplex lets both sides send at the same time
quiz.explain: Data is the information; a signal is its physical carrier. The medium is physical, and simplex is one direction only.

lessons.title: Networks and Topologies
lessons.content:
Think about how roads connect the villages of a union in Bangladesh. In one union, every village has a direct road to every other village. In another, all roads go to the bazar in the middle, and to get from one village to another you pass through the bazar. In a third, there is one long main road and all villages sit along it. Each layout has good and bad sides: cost of building, what happens when one road floods, how crowded the bazar gets. Computer networks have exactly the same choices. The shape of the connections is called the topology, and it is the first thing a network designer decides.

What a network is: A network is a set of devices connected by communication links. The devices are called nodes. A node can be a computer, a phone, a printer, a router, a switch, or anything else that can send or receive data. A link is the communication path that carries data from one device to another, whether it is a cable or a radio channel. We split devices into two groups: end devices (hosts), which are the ones people use, like your laptop or a server; and connecting devices, like routers, switches and modems, which pass data along.

Point-to-point connection: In a point-to-point link, the whole capacity of a link is reserved for just two devices. A cable from your laptop straight to a printer is point-to-point. So is the infrared link between a TV remote and the TV. Nobody else uses that link, so there is no sharing problem.

Multipoint connection: In a multipoint (also called multidrop) link, more than two devices share one link. The capacity is shared either in space (devices can use the link at the same time, each taking part of it) or in time (devices take turns). A WiFi channel in your home, used by your phone, your sister's laptop and the smart TV, is a multipoint link that is shared mainly in time.

Physical topology: Physical topology means the geometric layout of how devices and links are arranged. There are four basic ones: mesh, star, bus and ring. Real networks often mix them, which we call a hybrid topology.

Mesh topology: In a full mesh, every device has a dedicated point-to-point link to every other device. How many links does that need? Each of n devices connects to n - 1 others. That gives n(n - 1) connections, but each link is counted twice (once from each end), so the number of physical links is n(n - 1) / 2. For 5 devices: 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 links. Each device also needs n - 1 ports, so 4 ports each. Advantages: each link carries only its own two devices' traffic, so no traffic problem; if one link breaks, the rest still work; it is private, since others cannot read a dedicated link; and faults are easy to find. Disadvantages: lots of cable and ports, so it is expensive and hard to install. For 50 devices it would be 50 x 49 / 2 = 1,225 links. That is why full mesh is used only in small important places, for example to connect the main routers in a telecom backbone so that one broken fiber does not cut the country off.

Star topology: In a star, each device has a link only to a central device, usually a switch or a hub. Devices do not talk directly; they send to the centre, which passes the data on. For n devices you need only n links, and each device needs only one port. It is cheap and easy to install and to add new devices. If one cable breaks, only that one device goes off the network. The big weakness: if the central device fails, everything stops. Star is the most common layout in offices, schools and homes today. Your home WiFi router with its devices is a star.

Bus topology: In a bus, one long cable called the backbone links all devices. Each device connects to it with a short cable called a drop line using a tap. A signal sent by one device travels along the whole bus, and all devices see it. The ends of the bus need terminators so the signal does not bounce back. It uses less cable than mesh or star, so it was popular in early Ethernet using coaxial cable. Problems: a break in the backbone stops all communication; signals weaken as more taps are added, so there is a limit on length and number of devices; and only one device can send at a time without collision. Bus is rarely used for new networks today.

Ring topology: In a ring, each device connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop. A signal travels around the ring in one direction, from device to device, until it reaches its destination. Each device has a repeater that regenerates the signal and passes it on. Adding or removing a device means changing only two links. But in a simple ring, one broken link or one dead device can stop the whole ring. Designers fixed this with a second ring going the other way, or with switches that skip a dead station. IBM's Token Ring was an old example. Rings are still used in some metropolitan fiber networks because a dual ring can route around a single cut.

Hybrid topology: Real networks join these shapes. A university might have a star in each department building, with the buildings connected to each other by a ring or a partial mesh of fiber. Most of the Internet looks like a messy partial mesh of many stars.

Network types by size, LAN: A local area network (LAN) covers a small area: a home, an office, a school building or a campus. It is usually privately owned. Every host has an address, and data sent from one host to another inside the LAN stays inside it. Old LANs used a shared bus cable; modern LANs use switches in a star, and the common technologies are Ethernet (wired) and WiFi (wireless). Typical speeds are 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps or more.

WAN: A wide area network (WAN) covers a large area: a city, a country, or the world. It is usually built and run by a communication company and leased to others. A point-to-point WAN connects two networks over a long link, for example a bank's Dhaka head office to its Sylhet branch. A switched WAN has many switches and links and can connect many end points; the backbone of a mobile operator is like this.

MAN: A metropolitan area network covers a city. It sits between LAN and WAN in size. A cable TV company's network covering Dhaka, or a city fiber ring used by ISPs, are examples. Some books treat MAN as a kind of WAN.

The internet and the Internet: When two or more networks are connected, we get an internetwork, or internet with a small i. The Internet with a capital I is the specific huge internet that connects millions of networks worldwide. It is organised loosely in levels: international backbones run by big companies; provider networks that buy from the backbones; and customer networks, like your home or your university, that buy service from providers. Your ISP in Bangladesh connects upward to bigger providers and, through submarine cables and land links to India, to the rest of the world.

Protocols and their three elements: Remember, a protocol is a set of rules. It has three key elements. Syntax: the structure or format of the data, meaning the order of the fields. For example, a simple protocol might say the first 8 bits are the sender address, the next 8 bits the receiver address, and the rest is the message. Semantics: the meaning of each section. Does a certain bit pattern mean 'please resend' or 'all good'? Timing: when data should be sent and how fast. If the sender sends at 100 Mbps but the receiver can only handle 1 Mbps, data will be lost.

Standards and who makes them: For devices from different companies to work together, everyone must follow the same protocols. Standards are the agreed documents. De facto standards are ones that became common just because everyone used them. De jure standards are officially approved by a recognised body. Important bodies: ISO (International Organization for Standardization), which created the OSI model; ITU-T (the telecommunication part of the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency), which makes telephone and telecom standards; IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers), which made the 802 family, including 802.3 Ethernet and 802.11 WiFi; and the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), which publishes Internet standards as documents called RFCs (Requests for Comments). In Bangladesh, the regulator BTRC (Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission) decides things like which radio frequencies operators can use.

Real life example 1, a school computer lab: Imagine a school in Cumilla with 30 computers in a lab. If we connected them in full mesh, we would need 30 x 29 / 2 = 435 cables and 29 ports in every computer, which is silly. Instead, we put a 48-port switch in the corner and run one cable from each computer to it: 30 cables, a star. If one cable is chewed by a rat, only that computer goes offline. The switch then connects to a router, which connects to the ISP. The lab is a LAN, the ISP links it to the Internet.

Real life example 2, a bank across the country: A bank has a head office in Motijheel and 200 branches. Each branch has its own LAN in a star. Branches connect to the head office over leased links from a telecom company, which is a WAN. Important branches may have two links through different providers, so if one fiber is cut during road digging, the other keeps working. That is a small step towards mesh, chosen exactly where reliability is worth the cost.

Common mistakes: Mixing up physical and logical layout is common: a network might be physically wired as a star to a hub, but the hub copies every signal to every port, so it behaves logically like a bus. Another mistake is using n(n - 1) instead of n(n - 1) / 2 for mesh links; the first counts each link twice. Students also forget that in a star, the central device is a single point of failure.

What exams ask: Calculate the number of links and ports in a full mesh of n devices. Compare mesh, star, bus and ring with advantages and disadvantages. Differentiate LAN, MAN and WAN. Explain point-to-point vs multipoint. Name the three elements of a protocol. Name standards organisations and what they produce.

Recap: A network is nodes joined by links. Links are point-to-point or multipoint. Physical topologies are mesh (n(n - 1) / 2 links, very reliable, expensive), star (cheap, central point of failure), bus (one backbone, fragile) and ring (two neighbours each, needs care when broken). By size we have LAN, MAN and WAN, and many networks joined make an internet. Protocols have syntax, semantics and timing, and standards bodies make sure everyone speaks the same language. Next we see how protocols are stacked in layers.
key_points: A network is a set of nodes (devices) joined by links; links are point-to-point or multipoint.
Full mesh of n devices needs n(n - 1) / 2 links and n - 1 ports per device: very reliable but expensive.
Star connects every device to a central switch: cheap and easy, but the centre is a single point of failure.
Bus uses one backbone cable with taps; a break in it stops everything. Ring links each device to two neighbours.
LAN covers a building or campus, MAN a city, WAN a country or the world; joined networks form an internet.
A protocol has three elements: syntax (format), semantics (meaning) and timing.
Standards bodies: ISO, ITU-T, IEEE (802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 WiFi) and IETF (RFCs); BTRC regulates telecom in Bangladesh.
lessons.tip: Draw every topology yourself with 5 dots before an exam, and count the links and ports. Drawing makes the formulas impossible to forget.
lessons.task: Look at the network in your home or a nearby shop: router, phones, laptops, TV. Draw it, name the topology, and write what would happen if the router failed and what would happen if one phone's connection failed.

quiz.q: How many links does a full mesh of 6 devices need?
In a star topology, what happens if the central switch fails?
quiz.explain: All traffic passes through the centre, so it is a single point of failure.

quiz.q: Which protocol element decides the order of fields, such as address first then message?
quiz.explain: Syntax is the structure or format of the data.

quiz.q: A network covering one school building is usually a:
quiz.explain: A LAN covers a small area like a building or campus.

quiz.q: Which organisation made the 802.11 WiFi standard?
quiz.explain: IEEE's 802 committee made 802.3 (Ethernet) and 802.11 (WiFi).

lessons.title: Protocol Layering: OSI and TCP/IP
lessons.content:
Imagine your aunt in Sylhet sends you a gift of sweets in Dhaka by courier. She does not drive the parcel to your house herself. She writes a letter, puts it in the box with the sweets, wraps the box, writes your address on it, and gives it to the courier office. The courier office puts it into a big sack with other Dhaka parcels. The sack goes on a truck. In Dhaka, the steps happen in reverse: truck, sack, office, delivery person, box, letter. Each step only cares about its own job. The truck driver does not read the letter. Your aunt does not care which highway the truck takes. This splitting of a big job into stacked smaller jobs is exactly how network protocols are organised. It is called layering.

Why layers: Communication is a huge, complicated job. If one giant program had to handle everything, from the shape of the electrical signal to the meaning of a web page, it would be impossible to build, test or change. Layering splits the job into layers. Each layer does one part, gives a service to the layer above, and uses the service of the layer below. Two rules make it work. First, each layer only talks to the layers directly above and below it on the same machine. Second, a layer on one machine logically talks to the same layer on the other machine, by following that layer's protocol. Because of this, you can replace one layer without changing the others. Your WiFi can be swapped for a wired cable, and your web browser does not even notice.

Peer-to-peer logic: Even though data physically goes down through all the layers on the sender, across the wire, and up through all the layers on the receiver, each layer behaves as if it is talking directly to its partner layer on the other side. Your aunt's letter is written to you, not to the truck. That partner-to-partner conversation is what each protocol defines.

The OSI model: In the late 1970s, ISO developed the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model. It is a model, not a real protocol suite you install. It has seven layers. From bottom to top: 1 Physical, 2 Data link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application. A common memory trick from top to bottom is 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing'.

Layer 1, Physical: Moves individual bits over the medium. It decides the physical and electrical details: what voltage or light level means 0 or 1, how long each bit lasts (the bit rate), the type of connector and cable, and the direction of data flow. Most of the first half of this course lives here.

Layer 2, Data link: Turns the raw, error-prone physical link into a reliable link between two directly connected nodes (hop to hop). It groups bits into units called frames, adds physical (MAC) addresses of sender and next receiver, does error detection, flow control, and access control when many devices share the medium. The second half of this course lives here.

Layer 3, Network: Delivers packets from the original source host to the final destination host, possibly across many networks. It handles logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing, which is choosing the path. Your packet from Dhaka to a server in Singapore passes through many routers; the network layer decides the way.

Layer 4, Transport: Delivers the whole message from one process (running program) to another process on the other host. It splits messages into segments, numbers them, puts them back in order, and can resend lost ones. It uses port numbers to know which program gets the data, for example web traffic usually goes to port 80 or 443.

Layer 5, Session: Controls the dialogue between two systems: who talks when, and adds checkpoints (synchronisation points) so that a long transfer can restart from the last checkpoint instead of from the start.

Layer 6, Presentation: Deals with the format and meaning of the data exchanged: translation between different codes, encryption and decryption, and compression.

Layer 7, Application: Gives services to the user directly: email, file transfer, web browsing, remote login.

The TCP/IP protocol suite: The Internet does not actually run on OSI. It runs on the TCP/IP suite, which was developed before OSI was finished and became the real winner. Modern textbooks describe it as five layers: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport and Application. (Some books merge the bottom two and say four layers; the idea is the same.) The OSI session and presentation jobs are handled inside applications in TCP/IP. Key protocols: at the network layer, IP (Internet Protocol); at the transport layer, TCP (reliable, connection-oriented) and UDP (simple, connectionless); at the application layer, HTTP for the web, SMTP for email, DNS for names. At the bottom two layers, TCP/IP does not define its own protocols; it uses whatever the network provides, such as Ethernet or WiFi.

Encapsulation step by step: When you send data, each layer adds its own header (and sometimes a trailer) in front of what it got from above. Let us follow a short web request. The application creates a message, say 'GET index page'. The transport layer adds a header with port numbers and a sequence number, making a segment (for TCP) or user datagram (for UDP). The network layer adds a header with source and destination IP addresses, making a packet (also called a datagram). The data link layer adds a header with MAC addresses and a trailer with an error-detecting code, making a frame. The physical layer turns the frame into a stream of bits and then into signals on the wire or in the air. At the receiver, each layer strips off its own header, checks it, and passes the rest up. This is called decapsulation. It is just like the sweets: letter inside box, box inside sack, sack inside truck.

A small numbers example: Suppose the application data is 1,000 bytes. TCP adds a 20-byte header (minimum size), IP adds a 20-byte header (minimum size), and Ethernet adds 14 bytes of header and 4 bytes of trailer. The frame is 1,000 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 1,058 bytes. Of this, 58 bytes are overhead. The efficiency is 1,000 / 1,058, about 94.5 percent. If the data were only 10 bytes, the frame would be 68 bytes, but Ethernet also needs a minimum frame length of 64 bytes, so this one is fine, and efficiency is only 10 / 68, about 15 percent. That is why sending lots of tiny messages wastes capacity.

Addresses at each layer: Each layer that delivers something needs an address. Physical layer: no address, it just sends bits to whoever is on the other end. Data link layer: link-layer (MAC) address, 48 bits in Ethernet, usually written as six pairs of hex digits like 3C:52:82:1A:9F:04; it is used hop by hop and changes at every router. Network layer: logical address, like the 32-bit IPv4 address 192.168.0.10; it stays the same from source to destination (ignoring NAT). Transport layer: port number, 16 bits, which identifies the program. Application layer: names like a website domain or an email address, which DNS turns into IP addresses.

Devices and layers: A hub or a repeater works only at the physical layer; it copies bits. A switch works at the data link layer; it reads MAC addresses and sends the frame only out of the right port. A router works at the network layer; it reads IP addresses and chooses the next hop, and it builds a new data link frame for each link. Your laptop uses all five layers.

OSI and TCP/IP side by side: OSI was designed carefully on paper first, with clear definitions of service, interface and protocol for every layer, which makes it great for teaching. TCP/IP was built first as working software on real networks, and the model was written afterwards to describe it. OSI has seven layers, TCP/IP has five. In OSI, the network layer offers both connection-oriented and connectionless service; in TCP/IP the network layer (IP) is connectionless only, and the choice is made at the transport layer, where TCP is connection-oriented and UDP is connectionless. When engineers today say 'a layer 2 switch' or 'a layer 3 router', they borrow OSI numbers even while running TCP/IP. So you need to know both: OSI for the vocabulary, TCP/IP for how things really work.

Where this course sits: Data Communication focuses on the physical layer and the data link layer. That is the part where bits meet wires and air. The network, transport and application layers belong mainly to the Computer Networks course. We will mention them only when it helps you see why the lower layers do what they do.

Real life example 1, opening a news website on mobile data: You type a newspaper site address. Application layer: your browser builds an HTTP request, and DNS first finds the site's IP address. Transport: TCP opens a connection to port 443 and splits the request into segments. Network: IP puts source and destination addresses on each packet. Data link and physical: your phone's 4G radio wraps each packet in its own frames and sends radio signals to the tower. Inside the operator, the same packet hops over fiber links, each with its own data link frames. At the server, each layer unwraps its part. The page comes back the same way in reverse.

Real life example 2, swapping WiFi for Ethernet: Your laptop is on WiFi and you plug in a LAN cable because the WiFi is slow. Only the bottom two layers change: the frames and signals are now Ethernet over copper instead of 802.11 over radio. Your Zoom call keeps the same IP and TCP or UDP logic above it. This independence is the whole reason layering is so useful.

Common mistakes: Students often think MAC addresses go end to end. They do not: every router builds a new frame with new MAC addresses for the next link, but the IP addresses stay the same. Another mistake is saying 'the OSI model runs the Internet'. OSI is a teaching and reference model; the Internet runs TCP/IP. A third mistake is mixing up the names of the units: frame (data link), packet or datagram (network), segment (transport), message (application).

What exams ask: List and describe the seven OSI layers. Compare OSI and TCP/IP. Draw encapsulation with headers at each layer. Name the address used at each layer. State which device works at which layer. Compute overhead or efficiency for given header sizes.

Recap: Layering splits communication into simple stacked jobs. OSI has seven layers, the real Internet uses the five-layer TCP/IP suite. Each layer adds a header on the way down and removes it on the way up. Each layer has its own address: MAC at data link, IP at network, port at transport. This course lives in the bottom two layers. Next we go down to the physical layer and meet signals.
key_points: Layering splits communication into layers; each gives a service to the layer above and uses the one below.
OSI has 7 layers: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
The Internet runs the TCP/IP suite, usually taught as 5 layers: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Application.
Encapsulation: each layer adds its header on the way down (segment, packet, frame) and removes it on the way up.
Addresses: MAC (48 bits, changes every hop) at data link, IP at network (end to end), port at transport.
Hubs work at layer 1, switches at layer 2, routers at layer 3.
This course focuses on the physical and data link layers.
lessons.tip: Learn the layers with one real example you can tell as a story, like sending a parcel. If you can tell the story, you can answer any layer question.
lessons.task: On your phone or laptop, find your device's MAC address and IP address in the WiFi settings. Write which layer each one belongs to, and guess which one changes if you go to a friend's house and join their WiFi.

quiz.q: Which OSI layer turns raw bits into frames and does hop-to-hop error detection?
quiz.explain: The data link layer makes frames, adds MAC addresses and detects errors on each link.

quiz.q: With 500 bytes of data, a 20-byte TCP header, 20-byte IP header and 18 bytes of Ethernet header plus trailer, how big is the frame?
Which address stays the same from the source host to the final destination (ignoring NAT)?
quiz.explain: IP addresses are end to end. MAC addresses change on every link.

quiz.q: A device that reads IP addresses and chooses the next hop works at which layer?
quiz.explain: A router is a network layer device.

quiz.q: In TCP/IP, where are the OSI session and presentation jobs handled?
options: They are not needed at all
quiz.explain: TCP/IP has no separate session or presentation layers; applications handle those jobs.

lessons.title: Data and Signals
lessons.content:
Stand by a pond in your village and drop a small stone in the water. Rings of waves spread out, up and down, up and down, getting to the edge after a moment. The stone did not travel to the edge. Only the up-and-down pattern travelled. That is the key idea of this lesson. To send data, we never throw the data itself across the room. We make a pattern, a wave of voltage on a wire, of light in a fiber, or of electromagnetic field in the air, and let the pattern travel. That travelling pattern is called a signal.

Data vs signal again: Data is information: a number, a word, a song. A signal is a physical quantity that changes with time (or with space) in a way that carries that information. To travel through a medium, data must be turned into signals. The physical layer's main job is exactly that: turn bits into signals at the sender and signals back into bits at the receiver.

Analog and digital data: Analog data is continuous. It can take any value in a range. The sound of your voice, the temperature in Dhaka during the day, the brightness of the sky at dusk: all of these change smoothly, with infinitely many in-between values. Digital data has discrete values, a limited set of separate states. The text in an SMS, the number of students in a class, the bits stored in a file: these jump from one allowed value to another with nothing in between.

Analog and digital signals: Signals can also be analog or digital. An analog signal has infinitely many levels of intensity over time; when you draw it, the line moves smoothly up and down through every value. A digital signal has only a limited number of defined levels, often just two, like 0 volts and 5 volts. When you draw it, it jumps between levels in steps, like a staircase. Importantly, the type of data and the type of signal do not have to match. Analog voice can be sent as a digital signal (that is what mobile phones do today), and digital data can be sent as an analog signal (that is what a WiFi radio does). Later lessons cover all four combinations.

Periodic and non-periodic signals: A periodic signal repeats a pattern again and again over identical time intervals. Each repeat is called a cycle. A non-periodic (aperiodic) signal changes without repeating. In data communication we commonly use periodic analog signals (as carriers) and non-periodic digital signals (because the data bits themselves do not repeat in a pattern).

The sine wave, the hero of this course: The simplest and most important periodic analog signal is the sine wave. Picture the shadow of a point on a turning bicycle wheel, moving smoothly up and down. Every periodic signal, however complicated, can be built from sine waves, so if we understand one sine wave we understand a lot. A sine wave is completely described by three characteristics: peak amplitude, frequency and phase.

Peak amplitude: The peak amplitude is the absolute value of the highest intensity of the signal. For an electrical signal it is measured in volts. The electricity in your home in Bangladesh is a sine wave with an effective (RMS) value of about 220 volts; its actual peak is higher, about 220 x 1.414, which is roughly 311 volts. A bigger amplitude usually means a stronger signal, like a louder sound.

Period and frequency: The period, T, is the time needed to complete one cycle, measured in seconds. The frequency, f, is the number of cycles in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). They are opposites of each other: f = 1 / T and T = 1 / f. The power grid in Bangladesh runs at 50 Hz. So the period is 1 / 50 = 0.02 seconds, which is 20 milliseconds. Every 20 milliseconds, the voltage in your wall socket goes up, down and back to where it started. Units to remember: 1 kHz = 1,000 Hz, 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz, 1 GHz = 1,000,000,000 Hz. For time: 1 ms = 0.001 s, 1 microsecond = 0.000001 s, 1 ns = 0.000000001 s.

A worked example: A sine wave has frequency 100 kHz. What is its period? T = 1 / 100,000 = 0.00001 s, which is 10 microseconds. Going the other way: a signal has period 4 ms. Its frequency is 1 / 0.004 = 250 Hz.

What frequency really means: Frequency is the rate of change with respect to time. Change in a short span of time means high frequency. Change over a long span of time means low frequency. Two extreme cases are worth knowing. If a signal never changes, like a steady 5 volt battery output, its frequency is zero; a constant signal has no cycles. If a signal changes instantly, jumping from one level to another in zero time, its frequency would be infinite. Real digital signals have very fast jumps, which is a hint that they contain very high frequencies, as we will see in the next lesson.

Phase: Phase describes the position of the waveform relative to time 0. Think of two children on identical swings. Both swing at the same speed (same frequency) and same height (same amplitude), but one started when the other was already at the top. They are 'out of phase'. Phase is measured in degrees or radians. A full cycle is 360 degrees, which is 2 pi radians. A sine wave starting at zero and going up has phase 0 degrees. One starting at its peak has phase 90 degrees (a quarter cycle shift). One starting at zero and going down has phase 180 degrees (half a cycle).

Phase worked example: A sine wave is shifted by 1/6 of a cycle relative to time zero. What is the phase? 1/6 x 360 = 60 degrees. In radians, 60 degrees is 60 x 2 pi / 360 = pi / 3, about 1.047 radians.

Wavelength: Wavelength is another way to describe a signal, but it ties the signal to the medium it travels in. It is the distance a simple signal travels in one period. Wavelength (lambda) = propagation speed / frequency, or equivalently propagation speed x period. In a vacuum or air, electromagnetic signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km per second, which is 3 x 10^8 metres per second. In a cable or fiber, the speed is lower, roughly two thirds of that. Wavelength is often used for light in fiber optics, measured in micrometres or nanometres.

Wavelength worked example: An FM radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. In air, the wavelength is 3 x 10^8 / 100 x 10^6 = 3 metres. Red light has a wavelength of about 0.7 micrometres in air. A mobile signal at 900 MHz has wavelength 3 x 10^8 / 9 x 10^8 = 0.33 m, about 33 cm. Antenna sizes are related to wavelength, which is why FM antennas are longer than phone antennas.

Digital signals in a first look: Data bits can be shown with a digital signal. For example, bit 1 can be a positive voltage and bit 0 can be zero voltage. A digital signal can also have more than two levels. With 4 levels, each level can stand for 2 bits (00, 01, 10, 11). With 8 levels, each level carries 3 bits. In general, with L levels each level carries log2 L bits. We dive into this in the next lesson along with bit rate and bit length.

Why the world went digital: If analog signals are so natural, why do modern systems prefer digital? The big reason is noise. When an analog signal picks up a little noise, the noise becomes part of the signal, and there is no way to know exactly what the original value was; every amplifier along the way also amplifies the noise. A digital signal with two levels is different. If the receiver gets 4.6 volts when the levels are 0 and 5, it can safely decide 'this was a 5', throw the noise away and send out a clean new 5 volt level. Devices that do this are called regenerators or repeaters. Digital data is also easy to store, copy without loss, compress, encrypt and check for errors. The price is that digital signals need more bandwidth, which is the topic of the next lesson.

Real life example 1, the electricity in your house: When the electric wire from the Palli Bidyut line comes into your home in a village, it carries a 50 Hz sine wave. The ceiling fan, the light and the phone charger all depend on that frequency and amplitude. Phone chargers turn this alternating sine wave into a steady direct voltage. That steady output, as we said, has frequency zero. So in one charger you can see both a 50 Hz analog signal and a 0 Hz constant signal.

Real life example 2, Radio Foorti or any FM station: An FM station in Dhaka broadcasts on a frequency like 88 to 108 MHz. Your radio tunes to that frequency. The station's carrier is a sine wave of that frequency, with a wavelength of around 3 metres. The music itself is analog data, but it rides on top of the carrier by slightly changing the carrier's frequency. That trick, called modulation, comes in lesson 13. For now just notice that every radio station is defined by the frequency of its sine wave.

Common mistakes: Students often swap period and frequency. Remember: frequency is 'how many per second', period is 'how long for one'. Another mistake: forgetting to convert units. 5 kHz is 5,000 Hz, not 5 Hz. Many exam answers are wrong only because of units. A third mistake: thinking a high amplitude means a high frequency. They are independent; a loud low note and a quiet high note are both possible. Also, data type and signal type are independent: analog data can travel as a digital signal and vice versa.

What exams ask: Define analog and digital data and signals. Find period from frequency or frequency from period, with unit conversions. Calculate phase in degrees and radians from a fraction of a cycle. Find wavelength given frequency and propagation speed. Explain why a constant signal has zero frequency. Draw two sine waves with the same frequency but different phase.

Recap: Signals are travelling patterns that carry data. Data and signals can each be analog (continuous) or digital (discrete). Periodic signals repeat; the sine wave is the basic one and is described by peak amplitude, frequency (f = 1 / T) and phase (in degrees or radians). Wavelength = speed / frequency links a signal to its medium. In the next lesson we look at the same signal in two ways, the time domain and the frequency domain, and meet one of the most important words in this course: bandwidth.
key_points: A signal is a physical pattern (voltage, light, radio field) that carries data; the physical layer turns bits into signals.
Analog data and signals are continuous; digital data and signals have a limited set of levels. Data type and signal type can differ.
A sine wave is described by peak amplitude, frequency and phase.
Frequency f = 1 / T; Bangladesh mains is 50 Hz, so T = 20 ms. A constant signal has frequency 0.
Phase is measured in degrees or radians: a full cycle is 360 degrees = 2 pi radians.
Wavelength = propagation speed / frequency; a 100 MHz FM signal in air has a wavelength of 3 m.
A digital signal with L levels carries log2 L bits per level.
lessons.tip: Make a small unit table (Hz, kHz, MHz, GHz and s, ms, microsecond, ns) on the first page of your notebook and check it every time you do a calculation. Unit slips cost more marks than hard concepts.
lessons.task: Find the frequencies of three FM stations you know in your area and calculate the wavelength of each in air using 3 x 10^8 m/s. Then hold your phone's earphone wire next to the numbers and think about why radio antennas are about that size.

quiz.q: A signal has frequency 200 Hz. What is its period?
A sine wave is shifted by 1/4 cycle. Its phase is:
quiz.explain: 1/4 x 360 = 90 degrees, which is pi/2 radians.

quiz.q: What is the frequency of a perfectly constant 5 V signal?
quiz.explain: A signal that never changes completes no cycles, so its frequency is zero.

quiz.q: What is the wavelength in air of a 300 MHz signal?
quiz.explain: Wavelength = 3 x 10^8 / 3 x 10^8 = 1 m.

quiz.q: How many bits can each level carry in a digital signal with 8 levels?
quiz.explain: log2 8 = 3 bits per level.

lessons.title: Time Domain, Frequency Domain and Bandwidth
lessons.content:
Think of a cup of milk tea from a tong dokan, the small tea stall at the corner of the road. You can describe it in two ways. One way: you watch the tea-maker and write down what happened second by second. Pour milk, add tea, add sugar, stir, pour into the cup. Another way: you list the ingredients and how much of each is in the final cup. Two spoons of sugar, half a cup of milk, a cup of tea liquor. Both descriptions are of the same tea. A signal is the same. We can describe it moment by moment in time, or as a list of the pure sine waves (the ingredients) it is made of. The first is called the time domain, the second the frequency domain.

The time-domain plot: A time-domain plot shows how the amplitude of a signal changes with time. The horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is amplitude. This is what you see on an oscilloscope screen. A sine wave of 5 V peak and 10 Hz looks like a smooth wave going up to 5 and down to -5, completing 10 cycles every second.

The frequency-domain plot: A frequency-domain plot shows the peak amplitude against frequency. The horizontal axis is frequency, the vertical axis is peak amplitude. The same 5 V, 10 Hz sine wave becomes just one vertical line (a spike) at 10 Hz with height 5. All the information about the endless wave is in one line. That is why engineers love the frequency domain: it is compact, and it shows directly which frequencies a signal uses. A frequency-domain plot does not show phase; for that we would need a second plot.

Two or three sine waves together: Suppose we add three sine waves: 10 V at 50 Hz, 5 V at 100 Hz and 2 V at 200 Hz. In the time domain, the sum looks like a bumpy, complicated wave. In the frequency domain it is very simple: three spikes, at 50, 100 and 200 Hz, with heights 10, 5 and 2. The frequency domain makes it easy to see what is inside.

Composite signals: A single sine wave carries almost no information; it just repeats forever. If we only had one, it would be like a telephone that only ever plays one beep. To send data we must change something: the amplitude, the frequency or the phase. The moment we change a sine wave, it is no longer a single sine wave. It becomes a composite signal, made of many simple sine waves. So every useful signal is composite.

Fourier's big idea: Around 1807, the French mathematician Joseph Fourier showed that any periodic signal can be written as a sum of sine waves with different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. You met this as Fourier series in the Math III course. For data communication you only need the idea, not the heavy calculations. A periodic composite signal breaks into a series of sine waves with discrete frequencies: the fundamental frequency f (same as the signal's frequency) and its harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f and so on. A non-periodic composite signal breaks into a combination of an infinite number of sine waves with continuous frequencies; its frequency-domain plot is a smooth curve rather than separate spikes.

Square wave example: A square wave that jumps between +A and -A with frequency f is a good model of a digital signal like 101010. Fourier analysis says it equals a sum of sine waves at f, 3f, 5f, 7f and so on, only the odd harmonics, with amplitudes getting smaller: proportional to 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7 and so on. If you add only the first one, you get a sine wave. Add the 3f term and the shape starts to look squarer. Add 5f and 7f and the edges get sharper. A perfect square wave with instant jumps would need infinitely many harmonics, which matches what we said last lesson: an instant change means infinite frequency.

Bandwidth of a signal: The range of frequencies contained in a composite signal is its bandwidth. It is the difference between the highest and the lowest frequency. Bandwidth B = f_high - f_low. Example: a periodic signal is made of sine waves at 100, 300, 500, 700 and 900 Hz. Its bandwidth is 900 - 100 = 800 Hz. Another example: a signal has bandwidth 20 Hz and its highest frequency is 60 Hz. Then the lowest is 60 - 20 = 40 Hz. Human voice used in telephones is carried roughly in the band 300 to 3,400 Hz, so the bandwidth is about 3,100 Hz. Human hearing goes roughly from 20 Hz to 20 kHz, about 20 kHz bandwidth, which is why music quality needs much more.

Two meanings of bandwidth: Be careful: the word bandwidth is used in two ways. Bandwidth in hertz is the range of frequencies in a signal or the range a channel can pass. Bandwidth in bits per second is the number of bits per second a channel or link can carry, as in 'my internet bandwidth is 20 Mbps'. They are related: more hertz of bandwidth allows more bits per second, and the exact relation is given by Nyquist and Shannon in lesson 7. In this lesson we mean hertz.

Channels act like sieves: A medium does not pass every frequency equally. A copper pair, a coaxial cable, a radio channel or an amplifier lets some frequencies through well and weakens or blocks others, just like a sieve in the kitchen lets fine flour through and keeps the lumps. So a channel also has a bandwidth: the range of frequencies it passes without losing too much strength. When a composite signal goes through a channel, any of its ingredient frequencies that fall outside the channel's bandwidth are lost, and the signal that comes out has a different shape. Example: if a channel passes 1,000 to 2,000 Hz and our signal contains 500, 1,500 and 2,500 Hz, only the 1,500 Hz part survives. For good communication, the signal's important frequencies must sit inside the channel's bandwidth. This simple sieve idea explains why digital signals get rounded corners on long cables and why every radio service gets its own frequency band.

Digital signals in detail: Now let us measure digital signals. The bit rate is the number of bits sent in one second, in bits per second (bps). 1 kbps = 1,000 bps, 1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bps. The bit interval is the time for one bit: 1 / bit rate. The bit length is the distance one bit occupies on the medium: propagation speed x bit duration.

Worked example 1, bit rate for a text page: A page has on average 24 lines with 80 characters per line, and each character uses 8 bits. If we want to send 100 pages per second, the bit rate is 100 x 24 x 80 x 8 = 1,536,000 bps, which is 1.536 Mbps.

Worked example 2, digitized voice: Voice in a telephone is sampled 8,000 times per second (we will see why in lesson 10), and each sample is stored as 8 bits. The bit rate is 8,000 x 8 = 64,000 bps = 64 kbps. This number appears again and again in telephone systems.

Worked example 3, bit length: On a copper cable where the signal speed is 2 x 10^8 m/s, a 1 Mbps signal has a bit duration of 1 microsecond. The bit length is 2 x 10^8 x 10^-6 = 200 m. So at any moment, a 1 km cable holds about 5 bits in flight.

Levels and bits per level: If a signal has L levels, each level carries log2 L bits. Two levels carry 1 bit. Four levels carry 2 bits. If a digital signal has 8 levels, how many bits are needed per level? log2 8 = 3. If it has 9 levels, log2 9 is about 3.17, but we cannot send a fraction of a bit per level, so we would use 4 bits per level, or more commonly, designers simply choose a power of 2 levels.

Baseband transmission: A digital signal, as we saw with the square wave, is a composite signal with a very wide bandwidth, theoretically from 0 to infinity. Baseband transmission means sending a digital signal over a channel without changing it to an analog signal. It needs a low-pass channel: a channel whose bandwidth starts at 0 Hz. A dedicated wire between two computers is roughly a low-pass channel. In practice we cannot have infinite bandwidth, so we keep only the most important part of the spectrum. A rough rule from the theory: to send n bps with baseband, the minimum bandwidth needed is about n / 2 Hz, if we keep only the first harmonic. Keeping the 3rd and 5th harmonics gives a sharper signal but needs about 3n / 2 and 5n / 2 Hz.

Broadband transmission (using modulation): Many channels are band-pass: they pass only a band of frequencies that does not start at zero, like a radio channel between 2.40 and 2.48 GHz. A digital signal cannot go through such a channel directly. So we take a sine wave carrier at a suitable frequency and change it according to the bits. This is called modulation, and the result is an analog signal that fits the band. This is broadband transmission. Your phone, WiFi, satellite TV and cable modems all do this. Lessons 12 and 13 explain how.

Real life example 1, the telephone line: The old landline from BTCL to your home was designed to carry human voice in about 300 to 3,400 Hz. That is a bandwidth of about 3.1 kHz. When people used dial-up modems to get internet over this line, the modem had to fit data into that small voice band, which is why dial-up speeds stayed tiny compared to today.

Real life example 2, the equaliser on a music app: A music app's equaliser shows sliders for bass (around 60 Hz), mid frequencies and treble (several kHz). Moving a slider changes the strength of those frequencies. You are working directly in the frequency domain! A song is a composite signal, and the equaliser shows its ingredient frequencies.

Common mistakes: Students often think bandwidth is the highest frequency. It is the range: highest minus lowest. Another mistake is mixing up bandwidth in hertz and bandwidth in bits per second. Also, students sometimes say a square wave has only one frequency. It has a fundamental plus infinitely many odd harmonics. Finally, baseband does not mean 'slow'; Ethernet over copper is baseband and runs at gigabits.

What exams ask: Draw the time-domain and frequency-domain plots of a sine wave and of a sum of sine waves. Find the bandwidth of a composite signal. Find the missing lowest or highest frequency given bandwidth. Calculate bit rate for text, voice or video. Calculate bit duration and bit length. Explain baseband vs broadband transmission and low-pass vs band-pass channels.

Recap: The time domain shows a signal moment by moment; the frequency domain shows its ingredient sine waves. Every useful signal is composite, and Fourier analysis breaks it into sine waves. Bandwidth (Hz) = highest - lowest frequency. Digital signals are measured by bit rate, bit duration and bit length, and L levels carry log2 L bits each. Baseband sends digital signals directly over a low-pass channel; broadband modulates a carrier to use a band-pass channel. Next: what goes wrong as signals travel.
key_points: Time domain shows amplitude against time; frequency domain shows peak amplitude against frequency.
Any useful signal is composite; Fourier analysis writes it as a sum of sine waves.
A square wave of frequency f contains f, 3f, 5f and more odd harmonics with shrinking amplitudes.
Bandwidth (Hz) = highest frequency - lowest frequency; telephone voice uses about 300 to 3,400 Hz.
Bit rate is bits per second; bit length = propagation speed x bit duration. Telephone voice digitized is 8,000 x 8 = 64 kbps.
Baseband sends a digital signal directly over a low-pass channel; broadband modulates a carrier for a band-pass channel.
'Bandwidth' means hertz for signals and channels, but bits per second when talking about link capacity.
lessons.tip: Every time you see a signal, sketch both views next to each other: the wave in time and the spikes in frequency. After a few times, you will start to 'see' frequencies in waveforms.
lessons.task: Open the equaliser in any music app on your phone. Play a song, then lower the low-frequency sliders and raise the high ones, and the other way round. Write down how the sound changes and which frequency range seems to hold the drums, the voice and the cymbals.

quiz.q: A signal contains frequencies 200, 400, 600 and 1,000 Hz. What is its bandwidth?
quiz.explain: Bandwidth = highest - lowest = 1,000 - 200 = 800 Hz.

quiz.q: Which frequencies make up a square wave of frequency f?
quiz.explain: A square wave contains the fundamental and only the odd harmonics.

quiz.q: Voice sampled 8,000 times per second with 8 bits per sample gives what bit rate?
On a cable with speed 2 x 10^8 m/s, what is the bit length at 10 Mbps?
quiz.explain: Bit duration = 10^-7 s, so bit length = 2 x 10^8 x 10^-7 = 20 m.

quiz.q: Sending a digital signal over a radio channel from 2.40 to 2.48 GHz requires:
quiz.explain: A band-pass channel needs the data to ride on a carrier inside the band, which is modulation.

lessons.title: Transmission Impairments: Attenuation, Distortion and Noise
lessons.content:
Have you ever played the game where a line of friends whisper a sentence from ear to ear? The first person says 'Rina is going to Cox's Bazar on Friday'. By the time it reaches the tenth person it has become 'Rina is going to the bazar to buy fish'. Three things went wrong along the way. The whisper got quieter as it passed. Some words came out squashed or mixed up. And the noise of the classroom mixed in. Signals on cables and in the air suffer the same three problems. Engineers call them impairments: attenuation, distortion and noise. What is sent is never exactly what is received. This lesson explains each problem, how we measure it, and what we do about it.

Why this matters: The whole job of the receiver is to look at a damaged signal and guess what was sent. If the damage is small, the guess is always right. If the damage is big, bits flip, a 0 becomes a 1, and we get errors. Understanding impairments tells us how long a cable can be, where to put amplifiers, how fast we can send, and why error detection (lessons 21 to 23) is needed at all.

Attenuation, the loss of energy: When a signal travels through a medium, it loses energy, because it has to overcome the resistance of the medium. In a wire, some electrical energy turns into heat; that is why a long cable gets very slightly warm. In the air, the energy spreads out over a bigger and bigger area, like the rings in a pond getting weaker. The further the signal goes, the weaker it gets. This loss of strength is called attenuation.

The fix for attenuation: To make up for the loss, we use amplifiers, which boost the strength of an analog signal, and repeaters (regenerators), which read a digital signal and create a fresh clean copy. A long fiber link under the sea or a long copper line along a highway has amplifiers or repeaters placed at regular distances.

The decibel: To measure how much a signal has lost or gained, engineers use the decibel (dB). The decibel compares two power levels: dB = 10 log10 (P2 / P1), where P1 is the power at the start and P2 is the power at the end. If the signal gets weaker, P2 is smaller than P1, the ratio is less than 1, and the dB value is negative. If the signal is amplified, dB is positive. Why logarithms? Because signals change strength by huge factors, from a watt in a transmitter to billionths of a watt at a receiver. A logarithm turns huge ratios into small, easy numbers, and it turns multiplication into addition.

Worked example 1, half the power: A signal travels through a cable and its power drops to half: P2 = 0.5 P1. Then dB = 10 log10 (0.5) = 10 x (-0.3) = -3 dB. So '3 dB loss' means 'half the power is gone'. That is a number every engineer remembers. Losing 10 dB means the power became one tenth. Losing 20 dB means one hundredth.

Worked example 2, gain: An amplifier increases the power 100 times. Gain = 10 log10 (100) = 10 x 2 = 20 dB.

Worked example 3, adding along a path: Here is why decibels are so handy. A signal travels from point 1 to point 4. From 1 to 2 the cable loses 3 dB. From 2 to 3 an amplifier gains 7 dB. From 3 to 4 another cable loses 3 dB. Total: -3 + 7 - 3 = +1 dB. Just add! Without decibels we would have to multiply power ratios: 0.5 x 5.01 x 0.5.

Voltage decibels: Sometimes we measure voltage instead of power. Since power is proportional to voltage squared, the formula becomes dB = 20 log10 (V2 / V1). Halving the voltage is -6 dB.

dBm, an absolute unit: Engineers also write power relative to 1 milliwatt: dBm = 10 log10 (P in mW). 1 mW is 0 dBm, 10 mW is 10 dBm, 100 mW is 20 dBm, and 0.001 mW is -30 dBm. Phones often show received signal strength in dBm, typically somewhere around -50 to -110 dBm; a less negative number means a stronger signal. Example: a signal is -30 dBm at the receiver. Its power is 10^(-30/10) mW = 0.001 mW.

Loss per kilometre: Cables are often rated in dB per km. A cable that loses 0.3 dB/km over 5 km loses 1.5 dB in total. If the signal enters at 2 mW, the output is P2 = 2 x 10^(-1.5/10) mW, which is about 2 x 0.71 = 1.42 mW. Note: the loss also depends on frequency; higher frequencies usually attenuate more in copper, which is part of the next problem.

Distortion, the change of shape: Distortion means the signal changes its form or shape. It happens to composite signals, which, as we know, are made of many frequency components. Each component has its own propagation speed through a medium and its own delay. If the components arrive at slightly different times, they no longer line up the way they did at the sender. In other words, their phases at the receiver differ from their phases at the sender. When you add them up again, you get a different shape. A sharp square digital pulse arrives smeared out and rounded. If the smearing is bad, one bit's pulse spills into the next bit's time slot, which is called intersymbol interference. Distortion gets worse with longer distances and higher bit rates.

A picture for distortion: Imagine a group of students running from school to the playground holding hands in a straight line. Some run faster, some slower. At the start they form a neat line. By the time they reach the field, the line is bent and stretched. Nobody was lost, but the shape is ruined. That is distortion.

Noise, the unwanted extra: Noise is any unwanted signal added to the one we sent. Several types matter. Thermal noise comes from the random motion of electrons in a wire, which creates an extra tiny signal; it exists in every conductor above absolute zero and cannot be removed completely. Induced noise comes from outside sources such as motors, fluorescent lights and other appliances; the devices act like transmitting antennas and the cable acts like a receiving antenna. Crosstalk is the effect of one wire on another nearby: one wire acts as a sending antenna and the other as the receiving antenna. You may have heard someone else's faint conversation on an old landline; that was crosstalk. Impulse noise is a spike, a signal with high energy for a very short time, from power lines, lightning or switching heavy equipment. Impulse noise can wipe out several bits in a row.

Signal-to-noise ratio: To decide whether the noise is a problem, we compare it with the signal. The signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = average signal power / average noise power. A high SNR means the signal is much stronger than the noise: good. A low SNR means the noise is close to the signal: bad. Because SNR is a ratio of two powers, it is usually given in decibels: SNR_dB = 10 log10 (SNR).

SNR worked example: The power of a signal is 10 mW and the noise is 1 microwatt (0.001 mW). SNR = 10 / 0.001 = 10,000. SNR_dB = 10 log10 (10,000) = 10 x 4 = 40 dB. Going the other way: if SNR_dB is 36, then SNR = 10^(3.6), about 3,981. For a noiseless channel the SNR would be infinite, which is only a theoretical idea.

Fighting noise in practice: We cannot remove thermal noise, but we can keep other noise out and keep the signal strong. Twisting the two wires of a pair makes outside noise hit both wires almost equally, so it cancels at the receiver (lesson 17 explains how). A metal shield or braid around a cable blocks much induced noise; that is why the cable from a dish antenna is coaxial with a braided shield. Keeping data cables away from power cables and motors reduces induced noise and crosstalk. Using fiber removes electrical noise almost completely, because light in glass is not affected by nearby motors or lightning-induced currents. Finally, when noise does flip some bits, we measure how often with the bit error rate (BER), the fraction of bits received wrong. A BER of 10^-6 means about one wrong bit in every million. Error-detecting and error-correcting codes, which we study near the end of the course, are the last line of defence.

Real life example 1, WiFi behind walls: In a flat in Mirpur, the router is in the living room. In the next room, your phone shows full bars. Two walls away, in the kitchen, it shows one bar and the video buffers. Each wall attenuates the signal by several dB. Meanwhile noise from the microwave oven, which also works around 2.4 GHz, and from neighbours' routers stays the same or increases. The SNR drops, the WiFi chip falls back to a slower, more robust way of sending, and speed drops. Moving the router to the middle of the flat improves SNR everywhere.

Real life example 2, the long-distance fiber: A fiber link from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar runs hundreds of kilometres. Good single-mode fiber loses only about 0.2 dB per km near the 1,550 nm wavelength. Over 100 km that is about 20 dB, which means the light power is one hundredth of what was sent. So long links put optical amplifiers along the way. Distortion matters too: over long distances, different parts of the light pulse spread out (dispersion), so high-speed systems need special techniques to keep pulses sharp.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the sign: a loss is a negative dB value. Using 20 log for power or 10 log for voltage; check which one is given. Saying distortion and noise are the same: distortion is a change in shape due to different delays, noise is an extra signal added from outside. Also, increasing the signal power does not remove distortion; it only helps against noise and attenuation.

What exams ask: Define attenuation, distortion and noise and their causes. Compute the dB loss or gain of a path, including adding several sections. Convert between dB and power ratio, and between dBm and mW. Compute SNR and SNR_dB. List the four types of noise. Explain why a square pulse becomes rounded after a long cable.

Recap: Signals weaken (attenuation), change shape (distortion) and pick up unwanted extras (noise). We measure gains and losses in decibels, 10 log10 (P2/P1), so a 3 dB loss is half the power, and losses along a path just add. dBm measures power against 1 mW. SNR compares signal power with noise power and is usually written in dB. Amplifiers and repeaters fight attenuation, careful design fights distortion, and good shielding and twisting fight noise. In the next lesson we use bandwidth and SNR to find the maximum data rate any channel can carry.
key_points: Three impairments: attenuation (loss of energy), distortion (change of shape) and noise (unwanted extra signal).
Decibel: dB = 10 log10 (P2 / P1); a 3 dB loss is half the power, and dB values along a path simply add.
For voltages use 20 log10 (V2 / V1); dBm is power relative to 1 mW (1 mW = 0 dBm).
Distortion happens because frequency components of a composite signal travel with different delays; it causes intersymbol interference.
Noise types: thermal, induced, crosstalk and impulse.
SNR = signal power / noise power, usually given in dB: SNR_dB = 10 log10 SNR.
Amplifiers boost analog signals; repeaters regenerate clean digital signals.
lessons.tip: Memorise four anchors: -3 dB = half, -10 dB = one tenth, +20 dB = 100 times, 0 dBm = 1 mW. Most exam dB questions become mental maths with these.
lessons.task: Walk around your home with your phone and check the WiFi signal strength in dBm (many phones show it in WiFi details, or use a free WiFi analyser app). Write the values next to the router, one wall away and two walls away, and calculate how many dB each wall seems to cost.

quiz.q: A signal's power drops from 10 mW to 5 mW. What is the loss in dB?
A path has a 4 dB loss, then a 10 dB amplifier, then a 2 dB loss. What is the total?
quiz.explain: -4 + 10 - 2 = +4 dB. Decibels along a path just add.

quiz.q: Signal power is 100 mW and noise power is 1 mW. What is SNR_dB?
Which impairment is caused by frequency components arriving with different delays?
quiz.explain: Different delays change how the components add up, which changes the shape: distortion.

quiz.explain: Crosstalk is when one wire's signal leaks into a nearby wire.

lessons.title: Data Rate Limits and Network Performance
lessons.content:
Think about a road from Dhaka to Mawa. How many cars can travel on it per hour? It depends on three things. How wide is the road (how many lanes)? How many different kinds of vehicles can you squeeze into each lane, small and big, packed tightly? And how bad is the road: potholes and fog force everyone to slow down and leave big gaps. A communication channel is the same. Its maximum data rate depends on its bandwidth (the width of the road), the number of signal levels we use (how cleverly we pack each lane) and the noise (the potholes and fog). Two famous formulas, by Nyquist and by Shannon, turn this into exact numbers. Then we will see the other side of speed: delay, throughput and jitter.

Why we need limits: Engineers and customers always ask 'how fast can this link go?'. Without a formula, people might waste money trying to push 1 Gbps through a channel that can never carry more than 50 Mbps. The formulas tell you the ceiling, and the gap between the ceiling and what you get tells you how good your design is.

Nyquist bit rate, the noiseless channel: Harry Nyquist worked out, in 1928, how many signal changes per second a channel of bandwidth B can carry without symbols blurring into each other: 2B changes per second. If each change (each signal level) carries log2 L bits, the maximum bit rate of a noiseless channel is: BitRate = 2 x B x log2 L, where B is the bandwidth in hertz, L is the number of signal levels, and the bit rate is in bits per second.

Nyquist worked example 1: A noiseless channel has bandwidth 3,000 Hz and uses 2 signal levels. Maximum bit rate = 2 x 3,000 x log2 2 = 6,000 bps. If we use 4 levels instead, it is 2 x 3,000 x log2 4 = 12,000 bps. With 16 levels, 2 x 3,000 x 4 = 24,000 bps.

Nyquist worked example 2, finding levels: We need to send 265 kbps over a noiseless channel with a bandwidth of 20 kHz. How many levels? 265,000 = 2 x 20,000 x log2 L, so log2 L = 6.625 and L = 2^6.625, about 98.7. Since levels are usually a power of two, we would choose 128 levels (giving 280 kbps) or reduce the bit rate and use 64 levels (giving 240 kbps).

The catch with Nyquist: The formula seems to say we can get any speed we like by adding more levels. In theory, yes. In practice no, because real channels have noise. With many levels, the levels are very close together. A little noise moves the signal from one level to its neighbour, and the receiver reads the wrong value. More levels means less reliability. Nyquist ignores noise, so it gives the limit for a perfect world.

Shannon capacity, the noisy channel: In 1948, Claude Shannon found the true upper limit for a channel with noise. The capacity C = B x log2 (1 + SNR), where B is the bandwidth in hertz and SNR is the signal-to-noise ratio as a plain ratio (not in dB). The amazing thing about Shannon's formula is that it does not mention the number of levels at all. It says: no matter how clever your encoding, you can never send more than C bits per second without errors over this channel. It is the speed limit of nature. With clever coding you can get close to C, and modern systems like 4G, 5G and WiFi come quite close.

Shannon worked example 1, extremely noisy channel: If the SNR is almost zero (noise much stronger than signal), C = B x log2 (1 + 0) = B x 0 = 0. You cannot send any data, however wide the band.

Shannon worked example 2, the old telephone line: A telephone line normally has a usable bandwidth of about 3,000 Hz (300 to 3,300 Hz) for data. Suppose the SNR is 3,162, about 35 dB. C = 3,000 x log2 (3,163). log2 3,163 is about 11.62, so C is about 34,860 bps, around 34.9 kbps. That is why dial-up modems over a voice-band channel stayed around the 30 kbps range in the upstream direction. (The 56 kbps downstream modems we meet in lesson 20 used a trick: one side was connected digitally, so the noise from one analog to digital conversion was avoided.)

Shannon with SNR in dB: If you are given SNR_dB, first convert: SNR = 10^(SNR_dB / 10). Example: B = 2 MHz and SNR_dB = 36. SNR = 10^3.6, about 3,981. C = 2 x 10^6 x log2 (3,982), about 2 x 10^6 x 11.96 = 23.9 Mbps. A shortcut for high SNR: log2 (1 + SNR) is about SNR_dB / 3, so C is about B x SNR_dB / 3 = 2 MHz x 12 = 24 Mbps. Close enough for a quick check.

What Shannon teaches about trade-offs: The formula has two knobs, B and SNR, and they do not behave the same way. Capacity grows in direct proportion to bandwidth: double B and C doubles. But capacity grows only with the logarithm of SNR: to add just one more bit per second for every hertz, you must roughly double the signal power. So once the SNR is decent, buying more bandwidth is far more effective than shouting louder. This is why mobile operators in Bangladesh pay huge sums at BTRC spectrum auctions: more MHz is the most direct way to more Mbps.

Using both formulas together: Shannon gives the ceiling; Nyquist tells you how many levels you need to reach a chosen rate. Example: a channel has bandwidth 1 MHz and SNR 63. Shannon: C = 10^6 x log2 (64) = 6 Mbps. For safety we choose a lower rate, say 4 Mbps. Nyquist: 4 x 10^6 = 2 x 10^6 x log2 L, so log2 L = 2 and L = 4 levels. This is how a designer actually works: Shannon first, then Nyquist.

Performance measure 1, bandwidth: As we saw, bandwidth in Hz is a property of a channel or signal. Bandwidth in bps is the potential number of bits per second the link can carry. An increase in Hz bandwidth allows an increase in bps bandwidth.

Performance measure 2, throughput: Throughput is how many bits per second actually get through.
